slides.title: Mizaj means temperament
slides.text: Unani tradition, shaped by Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine, describes four temperaments: warm or cool, moist or dry. Your mizaj is believed to colour your energy, appetite, sleep and mood.
The Breeze. Garam-tar, warm and moist. Sociable, generous, quick to laugh and quicker to forgive. Starts every project with fireworks, finishes some of them.

The River. Sard-tar, cool and moist. Calm, patient and loyal, the steady one in every family storm. Hates being rushed, loves a long winter nap.
The Earth. Sard-khushk, cool and dry. Thoughtful, detailed and deeply loyal. Remembers what you said last year, and overthinks it at 2 am.

posts.title: Garam vs thanda mizaj, explained

slides.title: Garam mizaj vs thanda mizaj, explained
slides.subtitle: It's not about whether you shout. Okay, it's a bit about that.

slides.title: Two scales, not one
slides.text: Unani tradition reads temperament on two scales: garam or sard (warm or cool) and tar or khushk (moist or dry). Combine them and you get four mizaj. 'Garam mizaj' in the family sense is only half the story.
Garam-tar. Warm energy wrapped in softness. Your gussa is a matchstick in the rain: it flares for a second, then you're offering everyone chai.
Garam-khushk. The original 'garam mizaj'. Quick heat, sharp words, cools fast. Tradition suggests keeping a cooling snack close so hunger never lights the fuse.
Sard-tar. The thandi chhaon of the family. Slow to anger, slow to rush, and the reason every family argument eventually calms down.
Sard-khushk. Cool outside, a thousand thoughts inside. Feels everything, shows little. Many find warm, regular meals help them feel steadier.
